newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finland govt borrowing plans unchanged - official.
newsitem.headline: Finland govt borrowing plans unchanged - official.

text.p: The Finnish government's decision to buy foreign currencies from the market instead of via the central bank has not altered its borrowing plans for this year, a senior finance ministry official said on Thursday.

It does not mean that Finland will convert all foreign loans maturing this year to markka, but Finland will raise "100 percent or more" of its net borrowing needs in markka, said finance ministry finance councellor Inga-Maria Grohn.
The official projected 1997 government net borrowing requirement is 28.3 billion markka.
"Going directly to the market has not changed our borrowing plans this year, we will have the same policy as last year," Grohn said. "This has not changed our markka borrowing plan."
The total amount of gross borrowing in markka would depend on the market situation, which the ministry would review constantly, she added.
Last year Finland borrowed just 13 billion of its gross requirement of 167 billion markka in foreign currencies.
Grohn could not say if the government's total 42 billion markka foreign debt servicing -- 30 billion in maturing loans and 12 billion in interest -- might be converted to markka.
"We look at situations as they come," she said.

But she said borrowing in foreign currencies was now on hold, adding that it was "normal to halt foreign currency borrowing for periods" and that "we had considered anyway halting it or borrowing very little abroad".

The government said on Tuesday it had decided to let the Bank of Finland buy for the state the currency it needs for foreign debt servicing directly from the market, rather than channelling it via its balance sheet.
This means the extent of Finland's markka buying will no longer be visible through the Bank of Finland's weekly balance sheets.
